metadata.title: Push. Tag. Live.
metadata.source: DEPLOY.md (GCP Cloud Run CI/CD, dev environment); Dockerfile; deploy.yaml; medas-aggregation-frontend repo tree
metadata.description: Full walkthrough, in the order requested: (1) the complete GCP IAM / Workload Identity / Artifact Registry setup that lets the frontend reuse the backend's existing trust chain, (2) the React diagnostic app's own structure, (3) the pivot -- no pipeline existed to deploy or host any of it -- and the tag-based CI/CD pipeline (Docker + GitHub Actions + Cloud Run) designed to close that gap. No placeholder-typo narrative -- every command shown is the correct, working version.
metadata.note: Fully reconstructed from DEPLOY.md / Dockerfile / deploy.yaml / the app's own source tree -- no screen recordings or screenshots. GitHub-dark skin for GCP/CLI/pipeline beats, one Claude-cream cutaway for the app's folder structure, Claude cream skin for the bookends (INTRO, NEXT STEPS, OUTRO).

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW -- Claude cream skin, ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: Jambo -- this is Darshil. Developers push code to medas-aggregation-frontend -- the frontend for an AI-assisted diagnostic tool doctors use to review sepsis and diagnosis output. Here's everything that had to exist before a push could become a running service: the GCP trust chain, the app itself, and how it all actually gets shipped.

props.command: git tag dev-v0.0.1 && git push origin dev-v0.0.1
props.topic: GCP IAM · ARTIFACT REGISTRY · CLOUD RUN CI/CD
props.runningText: walkthrough: GCP setup → app structure → pipeline…
output: order: GCP trust chain → app → CI/CD pipeline

beats.narration_text: Start with somewhere for a built image to live. Create a dedicated Artifact Registry repository for the frontend, in the same GCP project and region the backend already uses -- project medas-499121, region us-east1.

lines: --description="Docker images for medas frontend dev environment"
props.caption: One Artifact Registry repo per environment -- dev, stage, and master each get their own.

beats.role_note: section A, step 2 -- find the existing WIF pool/provider
beats.narration_text: Now the identity path. The backend already has a Workload Identity Federation pool set up -- no reason to build a second one. List what's there: github-pool, and inside it, github-provider.

props.caption: Nothing to provision here -- just something to widen.

beats.role_note: section A, step 3 -- widen the trust condition
beats.narration_text: The provider currently trusts only the backend's repo. Widen its attribute condition to also accept this one, so both repos can authenticate through the same door.

lines: gcloud iam workload-identity-pools providers update-oidc github-provider \
props.caption: Always confirm with a follow-up `describe` -- read back what was actually saved, not what you meant to type.

beats.narration_text: The provider recognizes the repo. The service account still has to agree to be impersonated by it. Bind the shared github-actions service account so this repo's workload identity can act as it -- one role, scoped to exactly this repository.

props.caption: The SA's existing project roles -- run.developer, artifactregistry.writer, serviceAccountUser, logging.logWriter -- apply automatically. Nothing to re-grant.

beats.role_note: section A, step 5 -- GitHub Environment secrets + variables
beats.narration_text: On the GitHub side: a new Environment, named dev, holding two secrets and seven variables. Neither secret is a long-lived credential -- just the provider path and the service account email. The variables assemble the image tag and point the deploy at the right project, region, and service.

props.caption: GitHub's UI won't flag a missing variable -- diff this list against what's actually saved before the first run.

beats.role_note: section A, close -- the trust chain, assembled
beats.narration_text: Put together, that's the whole trust chain: the frontend repo requests a token, the provider recognizes it, the shared service account accepts the impersonation, and its existing GCP roles carry it the rest of the way into Artifact Registry and Cloud Run.

nodes.d: tags push, requests an OIDC token

props.caption: Same trust chain the backend already used -- one condition widened, one binding added.

beats.role_note: section B -- the React diagnostic app itself; Claude-cream cutaway
beats.narration_text: Before the pipeline, the thing the pipeline ships: a Vite and React frontend for doctors reviewing AI-assisted sepsis and diagnosis output. Auth gates the app -- no token, no diagnostic view. Everything doctor-facing lives under components: diagnosis editing, sepsis panels, an output table, a dialogue thread, a mic button for voice input.

props.title: Auth gates the diagnostic view.
props.calloutText: This is what a tag push actually ships -- a doctor-facing review UI, not a static page.
props.calloutSub: Vite inlines VITE_API_URL at build time -- the container never reads env vars at runtime.
props.sparkLine: Auth gates the view. Vite bakes in the config.

beats.role_note: the pivot -- stated only now, per the requested order
beats.narration_text: Trust chain: ready. The app: ready to ship. But nothing tied a code change to a running service -- every deploy was a manual build on someone's machine. The plan: a tag-based CI/CD pipeline. Push a tag, and a container gets built, pushed into the registry already set up, and deployed straight to Cloud Run.

props.name: medas-aggregation-frontend
props.headline: Trust chain: ready. Pipeline: missing.
props.tagline: no build step · no container · no host -- until this

beats.role_note: section C, step 1 -- the tag-based trigger design
beats.narration_text: First design decision: no deploy on every commit. Only a tag -- dev-v, stage-v, or a bare v for master -- triggers a build. Tagging is the moment someone decides this commit is promotable, not the moment it was written.

props.caption: One workflow file, three environments, resolved from the tag prefix alone.

beats.narration_text: The container is two stages. Node builds the Vite app -- the API URL and version get baked in as build arguments, because Vite inlines them into the bundle at build time, not read at container runtime. Then a clean nginx image serves only the built dist folder -- none of the Node toolchain ships in the final image.

lines: COPY package*.json . && RUN npm ci && COPY . .
props.caption: 8080, not 80 -- Cloud Run requires the container to listen on the port it assigns.

beats.role_note: section C, step 3 -- build, push, deploy
beats.narration_text: The workflow authenticates with the identity set up earlier, builds the image with the variables from the dev environment, pushes it to the Artifact Registry repo created earlier, then deploys it as a new Cloud Run revision -- using the same service account the whole way through.

props.caption: Five environment variables assemble one image URI -- the same table set up in the GCP section.

beats.role_note: section C, close -- the pipeline, end to end
beats.narration_text: End to end: tag, authenticate, build, push, deploy. One more step lives outside the workflow file -- some org policies block public access even with allow-unauthenticated set, so the Cloud Run service itself needed an explicit IAM binding for allUsers before doctors could actually reach it.

props.caption: Plus one IAM binding outside the workflow: allUsers -> roles/run.invoker, to actually open it publicly.

beats.role_note: the lesson, one beat -- card, no new component
beats.narration_text: So here's what exists now that didn't before: a shared trust path the frontend borrows from the backend instead of duplicating, a two-stage container that ships nothing but static files and nginx, and one tagging convention that decides dev, stage, or master. A developer's whole deploy action, after all of this, is two lines: git tag, git push.
beats.visual_intent: recap card: three columns -- 'trust chain (reused)' / 'container (2-stage, static)' / 'trigger (tag prefix)' -- closing on 'git tag && git push'

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW -- suggested prompt, read and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn: if your team already has one repo deploying to GCP through Workload Identity, don't stand up a second identity path for the next one. Widen the existing provider's condition, bind the new repo's principal to the shared service account, and reuse everything else -- the registry, the roles, the workflow shape.
